SRC_3: The filmgoing experience is different today than it was in the previous millennium.
People are more likely to see something on a big screen at home than at the local metroplex.
Films today rely far more on computer-generated imagery than films from 25 years ago.
Many people outside the movie industry think movies made in the 1990s and before looked and felt more “real” than movies made today.
Many people outside the movie industry attribute that difference to more computer-generated elements and the fact that movies are rarely shot on film anymore.
Video essayist Tom van der Linden argues that there is a deeper reason films no longer feel as real as they once did.
Van der Linden argues that viewers experience films with more than just their eyes and ears.
Van der Linden says movies today lack a sense of touch.

In his video essay “Why movies just don’t feel ‘real’ anymore,” van der Linden says that five reasons explain why recent films such as Jurassic World Rebirth do not feel nearly as immersive as Jurassic Park from 1993.
Jurassic World Rebirth is the seventh film in the Jurassic World franchise.
Van der Linden’s first reason is perceptual realism.
He argues that older films feature more deep focus.
Deep focus keeps background objects in focus.
Van der Linden says background focus lets viewers scan the frame and get a real sense of space.
Van der Linden says that ability is similar to how people perceive things in real life.
He says today’s films often put the foreground object in sharp focus against a blurry background.

Van der Linden quotes Noël Carroll saying deep focus and long-shot compositions invite audiences to scan the frame for meaning in a way analogous to ordinary perceptual experience outside the theater.
Carroll says those compositions are more realistic because they are more like ordinary perceptual experience.
Van der Linden’s second reason is the “cinematic look.”
He says the difference between Jurassic World Rebirth and Jurassic Park shows the importance of realistic environments.
He says the original Jurassic Park placed dinosaurs in a real-world environment.
He says Rebirth places dinosaurs in an overly cinematic, digitally exaggerated version of Earth.
He says that visual style pulls viewers out of immersion.
Van der Linden says digital manipulation lets filmmakers tinker with shots in the editing room.
He says filmmakers often do not commit on the day of filming to camera position, lighting, or background.
He says filmmakers can use digital tools in editing to change backgrounds, alter performances, and create camera movements that did not happen on set.
He says the over-manipulation of modern imagery creates a feeling of fakeness even when films contain real locations or real practical effects.
He says this is part of a bigger issue involving the amount of post-processing done on movies today.
He says modern filmmaking has shifted from making sure an image is exactly as desired before filming to making more, if not most, of those decisions after the fact in post-production.
Van der Linden’s third reason is indexicality, or the difference between film and digital.
He says celluloid film images were considered authentic representations of reality because light physically struck the film and created an image.
He says most films today are made with digital photography.
He says digital photography lacks film’s indexability because sensors convert light into an image.
He says a digitally captured image is a digital manipulation of reality rather than something physically created in the camera.
He says film has a more natural look because the physical shutter creates motion blur that makes action appear to move more smoothly.
He says digitally shot images can exhibit pixelated noise.
He says digitally shot films look sharper.
He says films shot on celluloid appear warmer.
Van der Linden’s fourth reason is haptic visuality.
Laura Marks believes film is experienced not just with the eyes and ears but with the entire body.
Marks calls that idea “haptic visuality.”
According to psychologists, haptic perception combines different ways of perceiving touch.
He says today’s films lack qualia, meaning “what it’s like.”
He compares the gritty, sweaty shots of Sorcerer from 1977, starring Roy Scheider, with a similar scene in Jurassic World Rebirth.
He says the difference between the two scenes is striking.
He says Sorcerer shows actors struggling in a realistic environment.
He says Rebirth uses flat lighting and vanity makeup that make the characters appear comfortable.
Van der Linden says no single reason explains why films do not look as real as they did 30 years ago.
He says the change comes from a combination of changes in the medium and in execution over the past few decades.
Van der Linden concludes that deep immersion does not arise from a single image but from a carefully constructed continuation of images.
He says each shot and scene builds on the others.
He says this creates sensory dynamics and feedback loops that map out spaces and add details and textures.

He says those elements, together with make-up, wardrobe, set dressing, sound design, music, and other filmmaking choices, can make a story feel more immersive, more vivid, and more impactful than the sum of its technical parts.
He says the goal is to be transported, moved, and touched.
He says the goal is to feel like something meaningful was watched and something real was experienced.
